title: Part Four: Fourteen Years Classified, and a Section That Says of Itself That It Verified Nothing
participants: Joint Inquiry of the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence and the House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence
House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence (2016)
Office of the Director of National Intelligence
National Commission on Terrorist Attacks Upon the United States

extractionLoop.stage1_upfrontSkim: What was gathered was raw reporting, and the gatherers said so. Part Four is a compilation drawn "According to various FBI documents and at least one CIA memorandum", which the Joint Inquiry then handed back: it "did not attempt to investigate and assess the accuracy and significance of this information independently, recognizing that such a task would be beyond the scope of this Joint Inquiry", and instead "referred a detailed compilation of information uncovered by the inquiry in documents and interviews to the FBI and CIA for further investigation".
extractionLoop.stage2_structuralCompromise: The gap the section documents is a real one and it is about the United States, not about Saudi Arabia. "Prior to September 11th, the FBI apparently did not focus investigative resources on [redacted] Saudi nationals in the United States due to Saudi Arabia's status as an American 'ally.'" The section states flatly that "the FBI did not treat the Saudis as a counterterrorism [redacted] threat prior to September 11, 2001", and that only after the attacks — "at least in part due to the Joint Inquiry's focus on this issue" — did the FBI and CIA establish a working group on it. The Joint Inquiry called the resulting gap in U.S. intelligence coverage "unacceptable".
extractionLoop.stage3_informationFog: Then the section itself became the fog. It was the Joint Inquiry's only wholly classified part: the rest of a 2002 congressional report was published and these pages were not, for fourteen years. A withheld section of a public report is an unusually generative object — it cannot be read, so it can be assigned any contents, and the assignment cannot be checked. By the time it was released the phrase "the 28 pages" had become a claim in its own right, independent of anything printed on them.
extractionLoop.stage4_monopolyWindfall: Release did not settle it, and the documents say why. Published on 15 July 2016 with "redactions to protect sources and methods", the section is hedged in nearly every sentence — "alleged by some", "may have", "reportedly", "could be linked, at least indirectly" — and its own Finding concedes that the Intelligence Community's information "has yet to be independently verified" and that neither CIA nor FBI witnesses could say "the extent to which such support, if it exists, is knowing or inadvertent in nature". The black bars remain, including inside the Finding. What fourteen years of classification bought was not secrecy about a conclusion; there was no conclusion to keep.
extractionLoop.stage5_merseyWhitewash: Two official answers arrived on either side of the release, and they point in opposite directions. The 9/11 Commission, which followed the Joint Inquiry, found at page 171 that "we have found no evidence that the Saudi government as an institution or senior Saudi officials individually funded the organization", and at page 218 that the individual Part Four treats at greatest length was, to its investigators, "an unlikely candidate for clandestine involvement with Islamist extremists". Ten weeks after the release, Congress went the other way: JASTA stripped foreign sovereign immunity for terrorism causing death or injury inside the United States, over a presidential veto, leaving the question to be proved or not proved in court rather than in a report.

closedLoopRatchet.inheritedFramework: Classification authority exercised over Congress’s own work product, and the Foreign Sovereign Immunities Act shield that kept the underlying question out of court.
closedLoopRatchet.newFrameworkCreated: 28 U.S.C. § 1605B, the JASTA exception: a foreign state is not immune where an act of international terrorism in the United States causes death or injury and a tortious act of that state or its officials contributed, "regardless where the tortious act or acts of the foreign state occurred".
closedLoopRatchet.closedLoopRecirculation: The secrecy manufactured the certainty. A section withheld in full was read as proof of what it withheld; when it was finally printed, the hedged text could not undo a conviction formed in its absence, and both the people who had demanded release and the people who had resisted it could quote it. The cost of fourteen years of classification was paid in credibility, and it is still being paid.

decoyVsLedger.viralDecoy: That the 28 pages were buried for fourteen years because they prove the Saudi government planned and financed the September 11 attacks, and that the American state hid them to protect an oil alliance.
decoyVsLedger.whyDecoyFails: The section disproves the "proof" half of that in its own words. It says the Joint Inquiry "did not attempt to investigate and assess the accuracy and significance of this information independently", and that it referred the material to the FBI and CIA precisely because testing it was beyond the inquiry's scope. Its Finding records that the Intelligence Community's information was information "much of which has yet to be independently verified", and that neither CIA nor FBI witnesses could identify "the extent to which such support, if it exists, is knowing or inadvertent in nature". The FBI's Executive Assistant Director told the same hearings: "To date I can't sit here and tell you that those ties go back, that we can prove that the Saudi royal family is sponsoring terrorism. But there's enough smoke that we are conducting several investigations." The Commission that came after found no evidence of institutional or senior-official funding, and found the individual the section dwells on to be an unlikely candidate for clandestine work. And the pages were not buried permanently: they were declassified and published by the House Intelligence Committee on 15 July 2016. But the opposite decoy fails too, and it is the one an atlas like this is more likely to slip into. "No evidence of official funding" is not "Saudi Arabia had nothing to do with it". The same page of the Commission report that carries the finding also calls Saudi Arabia "the primary source of al Qaeda funding", says the conclusion "does not exclude the likelihood that charities with significant Saudi government sponsorship diverted funds to al Qaeda", and records charities in which "al Qaeda operatives controlled the entire organization, including access to bank accounts". The finding is narrow, and it was written narrow on purpose.
decoyVsLedger.documentedLedger: A congressional report of December 2002 whose Part Four was classified in its entirety and published, with redactions, on 15 July 2016. Its Finding: that some hijackers in the United States "were in contact with, and received support or assistance from, individuals who may be connected to the Saudi Government"; that information, primarily from FBI sources, held "that at least two of those individuals were alleged by some to be Saudi intelligence officers"; and that much of what the Intelligence Community held "has yet to be independently verified". Its own statement that the Joint Inquiry did not test any of it. Its record that before 9/11 the FBI did not treat Saudi nationals in the United States as a counterterrorism priority "due to Saudi Arabia's status as an American 'ally'", that the resulting intelligence gap was "unacceptable", and that the FBI-CIA working group on the question was created only afterwards and partly because the Joint Inquiry asked. The 9/11 Commission's narrower finding at p. 171 and its assessment at p. 218. The committee's own characterisation on release — "not vetted conclusions, but rather unverified leads" — and the ranking member's hope that publication would "diminish speculation that they contain proof of official Saudi Government or senior Saudi official involvement". And, ten weeks later, 28 U.S.C. § 1605B, which did not decide the question but removed the immunity that had kept it from being decided.

citations.title: Joint Inquiry into Intelligence Community Activities Before and After the Terrorist Attacks of September 11, 2001 (S. Rept. 107-, H. Rept. 107-, December 2002) — Part Four: Finding, Discussion and Narrative Regarding Certain Sensitive National Security Matters, declassified with redactions and published 15 July 2016
citations.quoteOrFact: A 34-page scan with no text layer; downloaded from the House Intelligence Committee's own site and read page by page in a browser (report pages 415, 416, 417, 418 and 442). THE FINDING, at report page 415, in full as printed: "20. Finding: While in the United States, some of the September 11 hijackers were in contact with, and received support or assistance from, individuals who may be connected to the Saudi Government. There is information, primarily from FBI sources, that at least two of those individuals were alleged by some to be Saudi intelligence officers. The Joint Inquiry's review confirmed that the Intelligence Community also has information, much of which has yet to be independently verified, indicating that individuals associated with the Saudi Government in the United States may have other ties to al-Qa'ida and other terrorist groups. The FBI and CIA have informed the Joint Inquiry that, since the September 11 attacks, they are treating the Saudi issue seriously, but both still have only a limited understanding of the Saudi Government's ties to terrorist elements. In their testimony, neither CIA nor FBI witnesses were able to identify definitively the extent of Saudi support for terrorist activity globally or within the United States and the extent to which such support, if it exists, is knowing or inadvertent in nature." The same paragraph records that "Only recently, and at least in part due to the Joint Inquiry's focus on this issue, did the FBI and CIA establish a working group to address the Saudi issue", that "In the view of the Joint Inquiry, this gap in U.S. intelligence coverage is unacceptable, given the magnitude and immediacy of the potential risk to U.S. national security", and that "The Intelligence Community needs to address this area of concern as aggressively and as quickly as possible." WHAT THE DOCUMENT SAYS ABOUT ITS OWN EVIDENCE, at report page 416, and it is the most important sentence in it: "According to various FBI documents and at least one CIA memorandum, some of the September 11 hijackers, while in the United States, apparently had contacts with individuals who may be connected to the Saudi Government. While the Joint Inquiry uncovered this material during the course of its review of FBI and CIA documents, it did not attempt to investigate and assess the accuracy and significance of this information independently, recognizing that such a task would be beyond the scope of this Joint Inquiry. Instead, the Joint Inquiry referred a detailed compilation of information uncovered by the inquiry in documents and interviews to the FBI and CIA for further investigation by the Intelligence Community and, if appropriate, law enforcement agencies. A brief summary of the available information regarding some of these individuals is illustrative for purposes of this report:" What follows is a bulleted summary of FBI and CIA reporting on named individuals, written throughout in the conditional: of Omar al-Bayoumi, that the FBI "has received numerous reports from individuals in the Muslim community, dating back to 1999, alleging that al-Bayoumi may be a Saudi intelligence officer", that "FBI files suggest that al-Bayoumi provided substantial assistance to hijackers Khalid al-Mihdhar and Nawaf al-Hazmi after they arrived in San Diego in February 2000", and that "there are indications in the files that his encounter with the hijackers may not have been accidental"; of another individual, that "The FBI also received reports from individuals in the Muslim community alleging that" he might be a Saudi intelligence officer, and that "According to a CIA memo" he "reportedly received funding and possibly a fake passport from Saudi Government officials". Further items are given as what "may have" happened, what someone "claims", what is "believed", and what "could be linked, at least indirectly". On the discussion, at report page 415: "One reason for the limited understanding is that it was only after September 11 that the U.S. Government began to aggressively investigate this issue. Prior to September 11th, the FBI apparently did not focus investigative resources on [redacted] Saudi nationals in the United States due to Saudi Arabia's status as an American 'ally.'" ON PROOF, at report page 442, the last page of the section, quoting FBI Executive Assistant Director Pasquale D'Amuro: "To date I can't sit here and tell you that those ties go back, that we can prove that the Saudi royal family is sponsoring terrorism. But there's enough smoke that we are conducting several investigations to try to determine what other information is out there." Followed by the section's own summary line: "What is clear is that the FBI did not treat the Saudis as a counterterrorism [redacted] threat prior to September 11, 2001." The published version carries substantial black-bar redactions on most pages, including within the Finding itself; the classification banner on each page is struck through rather than removed.

citations.title: U.S. House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence, "Intel Committee publishes declassified “28 pages”", 15 July 2016
citations.quoteOrFact: Fetched and read in full from the committee's own page. It records that HPSCI, "under the direction of Chairman Devin Nunes (R-CA) and Ranking Member Adam Schiff (D-CA), approved publication of a newly declassified section of the 2002 Joint Congressional Inquiry", that "Following a declassification review, the Obama Administration decided to declassify the Joint Inquiry's only wholly classified section, commonly referred to as the '28 pages'", and that the Administration sent it to congressional leadership "with redactions to protect sources and methods". Chairman Nunes: "I support the Administration's decision to declassify this section of the post-9/11 Joint Inquiry. Because the information can be released without jeopardizing national security, the American people should be able to access it. However, it's important to note that this section does not put forward vetted conclusions, but rather unverified leads that were later fully investigated by the Intelligence Community." Ranking Member Schiff: "I applaud the Administration's decision to declassify the so-called 28 pages, a step I have been urging for several years. The American people have the right to know the full scope of the matters examined by the Joint Inquiry, and I have every confidence the public can assess the allegations raised in the 28 pages and the 9/11 Commission's conclusions on those matters. I hope that the release of these pages, with appropriate redactions necessary to protect our nation's intelligence sources and methods, will diminish speculation that they contain proof of official Saudi Government or senior Saudi official involvement in the 9/11 attacks. The Intelligence Community and the 9/11 Commission, which followed the Joint Inquiry that produced these so-called 28 pages, investigated the questions they raised and was never able to find sufficient evidence to support them. I know that the release of these pages will not end debate over the issue, but it will quiet rumors over their contents — as is often the case, the reality is less damaging than the uncertainty." The page also links "the declassified executive summary of the 2005 FBI-CIA joint assessment on Saudi Government support for terrorism", hosted at dni.gov. THAT DOCUMENT WAS NOT READ: dni.gov returns 403 "Access Denied" to automated requests and the browser pane here downloads PDFs rather than rendering them. Nothing in this dossier is taken from it, and nothing is claimed about its contents beyond the fact, stated on this page, that it exists and was released.

citations.title: The 9/11 Commission Report, chapter 5 "Al Qaeda Aims at the American Homeland" (Commission's own chapter PDF) — the finding on al Qaeda funding, p. 171
citations.quoteOrFact: Downloaded from the Commission's own site and read as extracted text. At page 171: "It does not appear that any government other than the Taliban financially supported al Qaeda before 9/11, although some governments may have contained al Qaeda sympathizers who turned a blind eye to al Qaeda's fund-raising activities. Saudi Arabia has long been considered the primary source of al Qaeda funding, but we have found no evidence that the Saudi government as an institution or senior Saudi officials individually funded the organization. (This conclusion does not exclude the likelihood that charities with significant Saudi government sponsorship diverted funds to al Qaeda.)" The sentence immediately following is part of the same finding and is usually dropped when the passage is quoted: "Still, al Qaeda found fertile fund-raising ground in Saudi Arabia, where extreme religious views are common and charitable giving was both essential to the culture and subject to very limited oversight." The page also records that entire charities "may have wittingly participated in funneling money to al Qaeda", al Wafa among them, where "al Qaeda operatives controlled the entire organization, including access to bank accounts". The finding is about institutional and senior-official funding. It is not a finding that Saudi money did not reach al Qaeda; the same page says it did.

citations.title: The 9/11 Commission Report, chapter 7 "The Attack Looms" (Commission's own chapter PDF) — the Commission's assessment of Omar al Bayoumi, p. 218
citations.quoteOrFact: Downloaded from the Commission's own site and read as extracted text. This is the passage that bears directly on the individual Part Four treats at greatest length. The Commission records the 1 February 2000 lunch encounter in Culver City and states: "We do not know whether the lunch encounter occurred by chance or design. We know about it because Bayoumi told law enforcement that it happened." It records that he "was in the United States as a business student, supported by a private contractor for the Saudi Civil Aviation Authority, where Bayoumi had worked for over 20 years", that he was "The object of considerable media speculation following 9/11", and that "Both we and the FBI have interviewed him and investigated evidence about him." Its assessment, at page 218: "It is certainly possible that he has dissembled about some aspects of his story, perhaps to counter suspicion. On the other hand, we have seen no credible evidence that he believed in violent extremism or knowingly aided extremist groups. Our investigators who have dealt directly with him and studied his background find him to be an unlikely candidate for clandestine involvement with Islamist extremists." The Commission reaches no finding that he was an agent of any government, and it does not say the encounter was innocent; it says it does not know.

citations.title: Justice Against Sponsors of Terrorism Act (JASTA), Pub. L. 114-222, 130 Stat. 852 (28 September 2016) — section 3, adding 28 U.S.C. § 1605B
citations.quoteOrFact: Downloaded from govinfo and read as extracted text. Enacted 28 September 2016, ten weeks after Part Four was published. Section 3 inserts a new 28 U.S.C. § 1605B into the Foreign Sovereign Immunities Act chapter: "A foreign state shall not be immune from the jurisdiction of the courts of the United States in any case in which money damages are sought against a foreign state for physical injury to person or property or death occurring in the United States and caused by — (1) an act of international terrorism in the United States; and (2) a tortious act or acts of the foreign state, or of any official, employee, or agent of that foreign state while acting within the scope of his or her office, employment, or agency, regardless where the tortious act or acts of the foreign state occurred." Subsection (c) permits a national of the United States to bring a claim against a foreign state under 18 U.S.C. § 2333 where immunity does not attach. Section 4 recognises aiding-and-abetting and conspiracy liability under chapter 113B of title 18. The Act names no country and makes no finding about 9/11; it removes a jurisdictional bar and leaves the proof to the courts.
